name: JA-16

lead: JA-16 is a laboratory antibody that targets myostatin, a protein that limits how much muscle the body builds.
It is of interest to people chasing a more muscular look, but it is used in animal research rather than as a product for people.

paras: By binding myostatin, the antibody reduces its growth-limiting signal, which in animal models allows muscle to be maintained or increased.
It is not an approved drug and no human trials are listed. Myostatin inhibitors are prohibited by WADA, and online products sold as myostatin blockers are discussed as a concern.

angle.text: JA-16 is of interest because blocking myostatin increased muscle size in mice. It is a laboratory antibody and not available as a medicine, and what people discuss for physique is the principle of myostatin inhibition.

lead: JA-16 (also written JA16) is an experimental antibody that blocks myostatin, a protein that limits skeletal muscle growth. Interest in it for looks comes from the idea that lowering myostatin activity lets muscle grow larger, giving a fuller, more muscular physique. [1][2]

It is a research tool used in animal models rather than an approved medicine. In 2003 scientists at Wyeth reported that an inhibitory antibody against myostatin given to adult mice produced greater muscle mass and grip strength, and concluded that myostatin acts after birth to restrain muscle growth. [2] A 2010 Circulation study infused JA-16 into mice with heart failure and found that it promoted greater maintenance of muscle mass. [3]

No myostatin-blocking drug for healthy people is on the market; Wikipedia notes that Wyeth's stamulumab (MYO-029) is no longer under development and that the World Anti-Doping Agency bans myostatin inhibitors. [1]

paras: Myostatin is a signalling protein of the TGF-beta family that restrains muscle growth; mice lacking the myostatin gene have more muscle. Antibodies such as JA-16 bind it and reduce its activity. [1][2] Other myostatin-targeting approaches, such as follistatin and soluble activin receptor, have also raised muscle mass in animals. [1]
Wikipedia adds that mouse studies suggest inhibition does not directly increase the strength of individual muscle fibers. [1]

Whittemore and colleagues at Wyeth (Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications, 2003) made an inhibitory antibody to myostatin and gave it to adult mice, reporting larger muscles and greater grip strength; they proposed that myostatin inhibitors might help conditions with low muscle mass such as sarcopenia, cachexia and muscular dystrophy. [2]

In the 2010 Circulation study by Heineke and colleagues, deleting myostatin only in the heart prevented skeletal muscle wasting in heart failure, and infusing JA-16 into heart-failure animals promoted greater maintenance of muscle mass. [3]

Myostatin inhibitors are on the WADA prohibited list. Wikipedia says athletes seeking such drugs turn to the internet where products sold as 'myostatin blockers' circulate, and quotes journalist Carlon Colker predicting that inhibitors will be abused once available. [1]
No studies found of JA-16 in humans. Animal work is described above; other anti-myostatin agents such as ACE-031 had preliminary human testing in the early 2010s. [1]
